Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view.

I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance.

My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses.
As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens.
It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music.
Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.
Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party.

In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “ Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth.
Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.
Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality.
Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages ) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky.
Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim.
If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.
Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well.
I used to watch “ passa passa ” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s.
These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability.
The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m.

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.
The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.
Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind.

More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines.

items.title: Independent journalism under siege in Georgia

s: Need for a unity became urgent in April 2025, after the law on approval of foreign grants
This article by Elli Kostika is an edited version of a longer piece, first published on June 11, 2026, by the non-profit journalism organization Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD).
This excerpt is published on Global Voices, with permission under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license.
Any use of images or charts by third parties requires permission.

As Georgia has dropped to 135th place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, iMEdD spoke with representatives of four independent media outlets about the challenges facing journalism in the country: imprisonments, attacks, “foreign agent” laws, and the struggle for survival.
Tamar Rukhadze, Deputy Director of Georgian outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti, describing the state of Georgia’s press, said:

Ι cannot remember any other period in Georgia’s recent history, since I’ve started as a journalist in 1997, with such a harsh and hostile environment towards journalists, media workers and civil society.
Georgia’s government, led by the Georgian Dream party, has intensified its crackdown on media by adopting a series of restrictive laws aimed at suppressing the country’s independent media.
Meanwhile, Georgian journalists have been facing constant threats, from legal challenges to physical attacks.

Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and a disputed election in October 2024.
Although Georgia has been an EU candidate country since 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream Party, founded by oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, has pivoted the country’s foreign policy towards Russia.

However, large segments of Georgia’s population remain pro-EU, and citizens have been protesting for over 500 consecutive days since November 2024, following the contested October 2024 elections and the government’s decision to suspend efforts to advance Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028.
As the struggles of Georgia’s independent journalists have intensified in this increasingly repressive environment, so too has their determination to survive.
Batumelebi and Netgazeti have paid a heavy price for their independence.
The outlets’ co-founder and CEO, Mzia Amaglobeli, was arrested on January 12, 2025, after an altercation with a police chief in Batumi, Georgia’s second-largest city.
Following a trial which press freedom groups denounced as politically motivated, Amaglobeli has been sentenced to two years in prison.
In December 2025, the European Parliament awarded her the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.
She remains detained under deplorable conditions.

Her eyesight — already poor before her imprisonment — is now almost completely lost, Rukhadze tells us, while her lawyers spent six months securing permission for her to visit a clinic, as medical facilities within the penitentiary system lack proper equipment.
In an interview with iMEdD, Rukhadze stresses the deep psychological effects Amaglobeli’s sentence has had on the newsrooms.
“ We aren’t the same as we were earlier before this imprisonment,” adding, “It’s a nightmare for every single journalist to become news.”
Rather than resorting to self-censorship, Batumelebi’s and Netgazeti’s journalists have persisted in their reporting.
She highlights:

The first thing Mzia did after her arrest was to send a message from prison, asking her team to continue their work as before — to do what they had always done and what they are known for: professional, ethical watchdog journalism that gives a voice to those who need it most.
Arrests and detainments are only one of the ways the Georgian government uses legislation against the country’s independent media.

Nino Bakradze, co-founder and editor-in-chief of iFact, tells iMEdD they have lost 90 percent of their income since May 2025 owing to a series of laws that have restricted the outlet’s access to foreign funding.

items.title: What telecoms leave behind when they exit a country

s: When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear

In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end.
But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure.
Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years.
Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company.

The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale.
Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar.
Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives.

Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end?
Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information.
In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable.

For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable.
Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so.
In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory.
Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story.
As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs.
They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access.
In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users.

Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts.
What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical.
It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences.
This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case.
After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets.
In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom.
In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity.
It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets.
Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building.
MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “ orderly exit ” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks.
The company has ended its operations in Syria, Yemen, and Afghanistan by 2025.
MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs.

items.title: Palestine is already living under the Big Tech authoritarianism the world is being sold

s: Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control
An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025.
Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO ).
For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction.
Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.
Surveillance, data harvesting, facial recognition, telecommunications blackouts, digital censorship and algorithmic systems are now woven into this architecture of control.

The genocidal war on Gaza has exposed the consequences with devastating clarity, where technologies built to collect, process and classify information have been absorbed into systems that surveil, target and kill Palestinians.
But Palestine is also a warning about what comes next.
Technologies developed, tested and refined under occupation do not stay there.
They become products, expertise and business models that circulate globally.

What emerges is a political economy in which military and intelligence institutions, technology companies, investors and governments converge around the extraction and processing of data as a means of exercising power.

This is one of the central arguments of Digital Domination, a publication of The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media ’s Maryam Abu Daqqa Fellowship, which brings together five studies on artificial intelligence, surveillance, data extraction and corporate power in Palestine and beyond.
The fellowship is named after Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian journalist murdered by Israel in Gaza in August 2025 while documenting life under siege.
Across different cases, the research points to the same transformation, showing how emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control.
It is becoming their infrastructure.
Israel’s surveillance industry shows this plainly.
It operates through intimate ties between military and intelligence institutions, private companies, venture capital and international markets.
Tools tested on Palestinians are refined, repackaged as commercial products and exported to the world as security solutions.
This is no accident of a thriving tech sector.
It is a political and economic system in which security technologies gain value precisely because of their capacity to monitor, classify and control populations.
The violence these systems enable is increasingly literal.

Investigations into Israel’s AI-assisted targeting systems, including Lavender, The Gospel and Where’s Daddy, have documented how machine-learning systems and mass surveillance data have been folded into the identification and targeting of Palestinians in Gaza.

A new film, NAZA, produced by The Guardian and built on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, details the secret systems used to select people for bombing in their homes at night, in the knowledge that their families would be killed, too.

At a military conference in London in late June, an executive from the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems presented a slide crediting its digital command system with 850,000 “real-time intel targets” across Gaza and Lebanon between October 2023 and the end of 2025.
The company has since tried to recast the figure as aggregate system activity, a claim that sits uneasily with the slide itself.
The significance is not that an algorithm has replaced human violence.
It is that these systems increase the scale, speed and bureaucratic distance at which violence is organised, while cloaking life-and-death decisions in the appearance of technical objectivity.

In June, Amnesty International and more than 100 other signatories warned that systems such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy dilute human responsibility and obscure international crimes behind a veneer of algorithmic objectivity.
The same architecture extends beyond weapons.

At 7amleh, we have documented how platforms suppress Palestinian speech, how state-linked actors use commercial platforms to shape information environments, and how Meta profits from content and accounts tied to illegal settlement expansion and violent rhetoric against Palestinians.

items.title: Protest as a pillar of democracy

s: Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have
This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy.
With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy.
You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings.
Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.
But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that.

Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.
Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have.

With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.
Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action.
Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement.

One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy.

In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.
Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out.
Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.
That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are.
And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression.
Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa.
This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia.
And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.
As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad.

The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability.
And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

items.title: When Big Tech becomes a tool of state control in Kenya

s: State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them
This post by Grace Kobare is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism.
In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South.
You can support this coverage by donating here.

On January 30, 2018, Raila Odinga held his symbolic “swearing-in” ceremony in Nairobi, and the government, through Kenya’s regulator, switched off the transmitters of KTN, NTV and Citizen TV while they were broadcasting live.
The Interior Ministry defended the move, saying the media had been given a security briefing in advance.
The stations stayed off air for days and were only fully back by February 9, 2018.
The 2018 incident was just one of many examples of Kenyan officials cutting off connectivity — particularly during times of unrest.
During the June 2024 tax protests, authorities shut down internet connectivity for around seven hours and arrested a large number of protesters.
The Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) also reported that at least three networks blocked the web version of Telegram during those protests, and the blocks were reversed the same day.
A year later, during the June 2025 protests throughout Kenya, a communications authority issued a directive to media houses to stop live broadcasts of the unrest, and Telegram was blocked again.
Access Now said this violated a High Court injunction against interfering with internet and Telegram access.
Given these incidents, it is no surprise that Kenya’s internet freedom record has worsened in recent years.
Freedom House found that in 2025 Kenya had the most severe decline of the 72 countries assessed during the coverage period.
Kenya’s experience is part of a wider pattern.

Freedom House found that global internet freedom declined for the 15th consecutive year in 2025, as authoritarian governments used censorship and offline repression to crush protests organized online.

Access Now’s 2025 report found that at least 313 shutdowns were implemented globally, and that in Africa the internet was shut down 30 times in 15 countries, with protests the leading trigger, followed by elections.
In Tanzania, an internet blackout was imposed after protests erupted on election day, October 29, 2025.
It was only partially eased on November 4, alongside a curfew.
An opposition lawyer said online mobilization was part of the reason for the blanket block, and protesters used VPNs to reach platforms such as X Spaces.
In Uganda, the regulator ordered all mobile operators and internet providers to suspend public internet access nationwide from 6 p.m. on 13 January 2026, two days before the general election.
Officials had publicly denied plans for a blanket shutdown beforehand.

The platforms themselves have been targets too: A Facebook ban followed the five-day blackout of the 2021 election and was still in effect in 2026, and Starlink disabled its terminals in the country after Uganda ordered the service shut down on grounds they were unlicensed.
Kenya’s case shows how state pressure on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them.
The June 2025 Telegram block came despite a High Court injunction.
The government has also tried to write that power into law.
In October 2025, President William Ruto signed the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it risks criminalizing legitimate online speech.
The Act also expanded the powers of a state committee, the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4), to make websites and apps inaccessible.
The High Court in Nairobi suspended key sections a week after Ruto signed it.
By July 2026, the High Court had declared the website-blocking powers unconstitutional.
The chairperson of the Bloggers Association of Kenya, Kennedy Kachwanya, told Human Rights Watch that the amended law poses an unacceptable threat to digital rights and freedom of expression.

items.title: Built for boats, adrift on land: Bangladesh’s Bede community struggles with a fixed-address system

s: Boats and people on the Turag River, Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Image via Flickr by Wonderlane. CC BY 2.0.
For nomadic Bede families on the Jamuna River in central Bangladesh, moving is a routine part of life.

A study published in May 2026 in the journal Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health looked at three nomadic settlements in Tangail district of central Bangladesh: Jugiyar Char, Palima and Char Nikrail.
It found that these families move several times a year, driven by seasonal floods and erosion, as well as searches for paying audiences.
However, climate change and increasingly unpredictable river conditions are forcing these communities to land.
The researchers conducted a micro-case study through 12 interviews and one focus group during Bangladesh’s 2025 monsoon season (June through October).
It describes displacement as an ongoing condition, not a single event.
“We cannot change the river, and we cannot stop moving,” one sardar, or community leader, told them.

A second study, published online in August 2026 in Dhaka University’s Social Science Review, highlights the dire environmental exposure and disaster vulnerabilities of Bede settlements in Munshiganj, calling for organized cooperation between government agencies and relief NGOs.
The Bede are a traditionally mobile community that has lived and worked on Bangladesh’s rivers for generations.
They have long been marginalized in Bangladeshi society, and many make a living as snake charmers, folk healers, sellers of herbal medicine and amulets, and street performers.
Historical accounts often trace the community’s roots to 1638, when groups arrived in Dhaka alongside the exiled king of Myanmar’s northwestern coastal region (then Arakan ).
It is difficult to get an accurate count of how many Bede exist in Bangladesh today.
Climate Watch, a Bangladeshi news site, has cited figures ranging from about 75,000, from the Department of Social Services, to roughly 800,000.
Families traditionally travel in boat groups led by a sardar (leader).
When they stop on land, they often camp on riverbanks or on chars, the sandbars that big rivers build up and wash away.
This is not ordinary migration.

Researchers from the study published in Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health contrast it with refugees who flee a single event: Bede families are almost always on the move, which makes them hard to reach for clinics, schools, and civil registers that assume a fixed address.
Today, many of these families are being forced to move away from their river roots and are settling on land.
Community members share that climate change has forced many to give up on the river as worsening floods, erosion, and storms make their former settlements uninhabitable.
They also said some canals and channels are drying up, making life on the water impossible in some areas.
In terms of income, one sardar explained that families stay about a month in one place and leave when audiences stop coming.

In Munshiganj, respondents told the Dhaka University team that demand for traditional work is falling, that stigma pushes people away from it, and that a recent ban on snake-catching has cost them income.
About 88 percent said they did not want their children to follow the traditional trades.

Concerning work on land, in 2019, leaders of the Bede settlement in Savar, near Dhaka, one of the country’s largest, told a police officer that poverty and dying rivers meant families could no longer sail to other areas, and that interest in snake-charming and other old trades was fading.
To expand Bede people’s economic opportunities, the Uttaran Foundation, a local NGO, has trained about 200 young Bede women, who now work in garment factories.
While both aforementioned studies are hyper-local and may not apply to all settlements, they reflect a tension between modern life, environmental realities, and traditions.
The Dhaka University study notes that many Bede families are landless and lack official citizenship documents, which limits their access to relief and disaster programs.

items.title: How a civic tech platform is helping women in Serbia get home safely

s: ‘[W]hat can we change in the spaces where people live, work, study and spend their free time?’

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
For many women and girls in Serbia, safety is not only a question of physical protection.
It influences their freedom of movement, their choices, and their ability to participate equally in public life.
This issue cannot be viewed separately from the broader social position of women and young people.

Reports by the Youth Umbrella Organisation of Serbia (KOMS) show that many young people experience insecurity, declining trust in institutions, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation in decisions that affect their lives.
The reports also document concerning cases of pressure, threats, and security risks faced by young activists who publicly advocate for social change.

At the same time, reports of the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality highlight that gender-based discrimination and unequal treatment remain persistent challenges in Serbian society, affecting women and girls in various aspects of their everyday lives.
Many incidents of harassment, intimidation, or discomfort in public spaces never become official complaints.
Some women do not believe reporting will lead to change.

Others fear judgment, social stigma, or consider their experience too minor to be important — but no experience is too small when it concerns the right to dignity, freedom of movement, and equal access to public spaces.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Varvara Lazarevic, the head of an NGO in Novi Sad, Serbia, to find out what can be done about this universal problem.

The NGO, Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad, and their project, SafeSteps, a civic technology platform where women can anonymously share their experiences of insecurity in public spaces, are presented here as an Impact Spotlight for the Serbian edition of the Digital Sparks Program.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Varvara Lazarevic ( VL): Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad has been working with young people and different marginalized groups for many years, with a focus on improving quality of life through education, information and support.

We founded Omladinske novine, a youth media outlet with both print and online editions, and since last year, we have also had our own podcast studio, where we work with young people and teach them about journalism, social media and media production.

Digital Sparks was important to us because it gave us the opportunity to connect areas we have been working on for years — communication, human rights and youth work — with technology. and turn them into a practical tool.
This is how Safe Steps was created.
The idea had been developing for years through my professional work, research and work with young people and women.
I wanted to explore how technology could become genuinely useful to people and give visibility to experiences that often remain unheard.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

items.title: Anthropic exposes AI operation that DRC journalists never knew existed

s: Disinformation surrounding DRC-Rwanda relations has weakened the diplomatic and public standing of both countries
Featured image from DRC media, created using screenshots from ACP's YouTube channel
In September 2026, Anthropic, an artificial intelligence (AI) development and research company, exposed a network of fake news sites targeting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The investigation revealed that large-scale, AI-powered disinformation campaigns have emerged at a time of conflict when trust in the news is already at an all-time low and resources are severely limited.
This revelation rang alarm bells for African media watchdogs.
The network coordinated around 70 AI-powered fake news sites and generated at least 318 articles on the eastern DRC conflict, relations with Rwanda, and contested mineral resources.
The operation was highly robust.
On X, coordinated accounts amplified content from the AI-run sites, mimicking legitimate media outlets and rewriting articles for different audiences.
According to Anthropic’s report, the LKM Company, a French advertising agency serving clients with strong interests in the DRC-Rwanda conflict, was behind it all.
They found no evidence of direct government involvement.

When Global Voices approached Hobab Watukalusu, a fact-checker, editor, and head of the training and research department at Soma Média Lab in Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, he shared:
Nous n’avions pas identifié cette opération dans toute son ampleur avant sa révélation.

Cela montre les limites auxquelles nous sommes confrontés face à des campagnes capables de produire, à très grande échelle et dans des délais très courts, des contenus qui peuvent paraître crédibles et s’insérer rapidement dans l’écosystème informationnel.
We hadn’t recognized the full extent of the operation before this revelation.
This highlights our limitations when dealing with campaigns that can rapidly generate large-scale, credible-looking content and quickly gain a foothold in the infoscape.
He added that local journalists on the front lines are struggling to keep up as new technologies make it easier than ever to facilitate massive disinformation campaigns.
DR Congolese fact-checkers face a litany of obstacles in slowing disinformation flows across regions.
Hobab outlines the fundamental constraints:
L'accès encore difficile à l'électricité, à une connexion Internet stable et abordable, ainsi que le coût élevé de la vie constituent des contraintes réelles pour les professionnels de l'information.
Ongoing difficulties in accessing electricity, stable and affordable internet connections, and high living costs pose real-world constraints for journalists.
In the DRC, where journalists are already overwhelmed by covering an active military conflict, analyzing potential industrial-scale, AI-generated content is virtually impossible.
Joël Kaseso, another journalist covering disinformation narratives, told Global Voices:
Des ressources existent, mais la plupart sont payantes.
Ce qui limite notre capacité à tout analyser dans ce contexte tendu où les relations diplomatiques et sécuritaires avec les pays voisins, notamment le Rwanda, ne sont plus au bon fixe.
Although resources exist, most are not free.

Amid this tense environment, where diplomatic and security relations with neighboring countries, particularly Rwanda, are strained, this financial barrier limits our ability to conduct a full analysis.

Kaseso has also identified a simple but critical methodology that most journalists use to navigate this situation: analyzing the author’s intentions, the source’s profile (anonymous accounts versus identifiable influencers), and amplification patterns.
However, this requires time and tools that many newsrooms don’t have.
Détecter qu'un contenu a été généré ou manipulé à l'aide de l'intelligence artificielle ne constitue que la première étape.
Il faut ensuite déterminer si ce contenu est trompeur, identifier sa source, comprendre comment il se diffuse et, surtout, établir dans quel objectif il a été produit.
C'est cette chaîne complète de vérification qui demande du temps, des compétences et des ressources.
Detecting AI-generated or AI-manipulated content is only the first step.
The next steps involve determining whether the content is misleading, identifying its source, understanding how it spreads, and, above all, establishing why it was created in the first place.
This comprehensive verification process requires time, skill, and resources.

items.title: Students air their frustrations anonymously online as emigration tempts many young people in North Macedonia

s: ‘Students don’t have to be members of a political party to create change,’ says founder of online media platform

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Students in North Macedonia are not the happiest group: a 2026 survey suggests that over 76 percent of current students are thinking of emigrating.
The main reasons for this being cited are “quality of life” and “finding employment suitable to professional qualifications.”
However, what if students themselves could change that?
North Macedonia, luckily, has people who decided to take their fate into their own hands and help students achieve a better quality of life, not only for themselves, but for many young people.

At first, Goshe Nikolov, at the time a student himself, founded Instagram-based student media, Studentarija, as an entertainment resource, where students from all over the country shared memes about studies and current events.
This outlet now has over 65,000 subscribers, which is a significant number for a country with 53,000 students.

As he comes to the Zoom interview with Global Voices, Nikolov already has nine years of experience running the most successful student media in the country, and with the help of his team of three, has launched a Digital Student Voice, an online platform that enables students across North Macedonia to anonymously report problems related to higher education and student life.
They were able to do it with the help of the Digital Democracy Initiative grant.
Nikolov has a wide smile and a confident attitude; he answers questions with the clarity that could only be gained by years of hands-on experience.
Global Voices (GV): Could you tell us a little about your student media outlet?
How did it start?
How did you manage to gain so many followers and so much engagement?
Is it only on Instagram?
Goshe Nikolov (GN): Studentarija started in 2017, when I was still a student.
I created it from my room in a student dormitory in Skopje.
At that time, Instagram was becoming increasingly popular among students in North Macedonia, but there was no Macedonian Instagram page specifically for students.
So I decided to create one, and quite spontaneously, in the end it got the name Studentarija, which it still has today.
In the beginning, the idea was very simple.
It was a place where students could share funny and relatable content.
For example, memes, funny videos, everyday posts and situations from student life.
So I could never have imagined that one day it would become what it is today.
Over time, the audience kept growing, and I think that demonstrated that there was a real need for such a space.
At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020, I started focusing more on the real problems and challenges faced by students in North Macedonia.
Students started coming to us with questions, asking for information and sharing their problems, because they often could not get the information or support they needed elsewhere.
That was when I really understood that Studentarija could play a much bigger role in the lives of students and young people in our country.
So I think the main reasons young people have stayed with us over the years are our openness, transparency, creativity, consistency and, of course, accessibility.
Students in North Macedonia know that they can come directly to us, that we listen to them, and that Studentarija is genuinely built around their experiences and their needs.
GV: So do you think it will remain only on Instagram, or are you planning to use other platforms for further development?

items.title: US President Donald Trump appears to wear makeup after apparent rash breaks out on neck, reports say

s: On Tuesday, a rash that reporters had observed on US President Donald Trump's neck in photos from a Medal of Honor ceremony at the White House one day earlier appeared to have been covered up.
One media source indicated the substance used was cosmetic makeup, although Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Barbabella, told the source the rash had been covered up by a "very common cream."
President Trump has worn makeup in public before.
He once wore makeup to obscure bruises on his hands, which White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, stated were inflicted from "shaking hands all day every day.
Trump himself has attributed the bruises to his use of aspirin, of which he says he takes excessive amounts.
Trump said, "They say aspirin is good for thinning out the blood, and I don’t want thick blood pouring through my heart.
I want nice, thin blood pouring through my heart.
Does that make sense?"

items.title: Monta publishes its 2025 EV charger ranking, including hardware performance

s: The Danish firm Monta published a performance ranking of electric vehicle (EV) chargers on Wednesday.
The firm analysed 260,000 EV chargers connected to its platform, which were located in Europe.
In the publication, the firm showed the chargers ranked by their "performance score".
The firm calculated this score metric from two parameters — the charger uptime, and the percent of charge sessions that went successful without hardware or software or user interruptions.
The AC — slower chargers — and DC — fast chargers — ranking was provided in two separate tables.
AC chargers performance was topped by a Mennekes EV charger, with performance score 94.65.
Among DC chargers, five charger models by Alpitronic took the top spots, with performance score reaching 96.54.

The Driven, an Australian news site, noted that '9 out of 10' of the top performing DC chargers from Monta's report were available for sale, and were in use — by Ampol AmpCharge and BP Pulse — in Australia.
The firm noted the published results provided motivation for EV chargers to adopt these benchmarks in marketing, and further develop their products to increase performance and uptime.

A volunteer Wikinews reporter reached out to Monta, and Monta has clarified that they also have some EV chargers on their platform in Asia, Oceania, and North America, however excluded them from the ranking due to small quantities.
Monta also noted they were planning to release quarterly EV charger updates in 2026, and yearly EV charger ranking reports with awards.
The Monta's EV charger ranking program was launched in June last year.
Monta won the best EV app/software at the E-Mobility Awards 2023.

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules

s: This past Friday, Justice Paul Smith of the Supreme Court of Queensland ruled that the City of Moreton Bay Council, immediately north of Brisbane, Australia, acted unlawfully when it removed several homeless people camping in public parks last year.

The court concluded the Council breached the law by providing insufficient time for the homeless people to find alternative accommodation and by disposing of their personal belongings without consent.

In the judgement, Justice Smith said the Council made "errors of law" finding that the Council's seizure and disposal of the property of eight homeless people at Eddie Hyland Park — including their tents and other personal belongings — without consent in April and May last year violated human rights.
Although the eviction involved eight campers at the park, the legal case was brought by eleven applicants who said they were affected by the Council's enforcement actions.
The judgement noted that the Council would still be allowed to remove campers from public parks provided this was done "lawfully".
On Friday, the Council published a statement noting that eight homeless people had taken the Council to court and linking to the Supreme Court judgement.
In that statement Council stated it would continue enforcing its ban on camping on public land.
Responsibility for providing shelter to homeless people rested with the Queensland state government according to the Council.
The court scheduled the next hearing in three weeks to determine relief and costs.
Basic Rights Queensland and the Queensland Human Rights Commission supported the campers in the legal proceedings.
The Council's actions followed its decision earlier in February last year to ban camping on public land, which made camping illegal on public land within the Council from March 12, 2025.

items.title: Australia grants refuge to five Iranian women's national soccer team players

s: Early Tuesday morning, Australia government officials issued humanitarian visas to five members of Iran's national women's football team.

The players refused to sing the Iranian anthem while at the Women's Asian Cup last week. if the visas had not been granted, the five players potentially faced serious punishment on their return to Iran, as Iranian media has labeled them "traitors".
Tony Burke, Minister for Home Affairs of Australia, sent a message on X on Tuesday stating that the five players were "welcome to stay in Australia, to be safe and have a home here".
The players are Zahra Ghanbari (captain), Fatemeh Pasandideh, Zahra Sarbali, Atefeh Ramezanizadeh, and Mona Hamoudi.
Tuesday afternoon, however, the rest of the Iranian national women's soccer team travelled to Gold Coast airport by bus.
As of Tuesday morning, authorities said these remaining Iranian women's soccer team members had not requested asylum, though were welcomed to do so.
Protesters surrounded the bus and some were lying on the ground to stop the bus, and had to be moved by police.

Due to reported threats from Iranian media and officials, in Australia, local police worked with the authorities and provided a safe place for the players to stay, as well as increased presence when the players were traveling.

items.title: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Julio Teherán retires

s: Julio Teherán, a two-time Major League Baseball All-Star, announced his retirement from baseball on Monday, at the age of 35.
The decision came two days after he was scratched from a scheduled start for Team Colombia in the 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) due to a shoulder injury.
Teherán had helped Team Colombia secure a 3-1 victory over Team Panama in the WBC before announcing his retirement.
Teherán had a thirteen-year MLB career, during which he primarily played for the Atlanta Braves, but also played for the Los Angeles Angels, Detroit Tigers, Milwaukee Brewers, and New York Mets.
He made his MLB debut with the Braves in 2011 at the age of 20 and spent his first nine seasons with the team, earning All-Star selections in 2014 and 2016.
Over his MLB career, Teherán compiled a 81-82 record, with a 3.85 ERA, 1.223 WHIP, and 1,260 strikeouts in 1,470.2 innings.
He had spent the 2022 and 2025 seasons playing in the Mexican Baseball League.

items.title: PM of Australia sends E-7A Wedgetail and air-to-air missiles to UAE

s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that, in response to United Arab Emirates call for help, Australia would deploy E-7A Wedgetail, a long-range reconnaissance plane, to help Gulf Arab states defend against attacks from Iran.
The Australian Defence Force said the plane is able to survey four million square kilometers with a powerful radar.
Government officials said the plane would be manned by around 85 Australian defence force (ADF) personnel.
Additionally, Australia would supply middle range air to air missiles, at the request of United Arab Emirates, that could down enemy's drones.
Foreign affairs correspondent at ABC News, Stephen Dziedzic, published a piece on Wednesday noting that from a legal perspective, Australia is at war.
He stated that not being an attacker, and not entering Iran, did not preclude Australia from joining a war.

The correspondent referenced article 51 from United Nations charter about "collective self-defence", which could involve, for example, providing support or intelligence to one of the participants of a war.
The correspondent raised concern that move could make Australia a potential target for attacks from, for example, Iran.

items.title: NSW government proposes rezoning to create residences midway between Sydney and Parramatta

s: The government of New South Wales (NSW), Australia announced plans to rezone the 113-hectare Burwood North precinct this Tuesday.
The plan included building 18,300 new homes in the area, and building a new metro station.
This would position the area as a residential hub between Sydney CBD and Parramatta, shortening commute times down to ten minutes, the proposal said.

With allowance for up to 42 storey residential buildings, the government proposal involved a requirement that at least 5% of the new homes were "affordable housing", offered at a lower rental price to lower income households.
Burwood North Station, scheduled to open in 2032, would provide easier access to retail outlets and businesses located near Parramatta Road, and reduce load on existing train and bus networks.
The proposal text noted it would create 3,900 new jobs to implement the changes.
The proposal was a part of Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy.
The NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was listed as a contact for inquiries and feedback.

items.title: US president Donald Trump demands the unconditional surrender of Iran

s: Last Friday, United States President Donald Trump demanded the "unconditional surrender" of Iran via his Truth Social platform.
The declaration came as the war in Iran had gone on for a week.
Trump has also demanded more "acceptable" leadership in the country.
Trump wrote that once "acceptable" leadership was selected in Iran, the US and its allies would make Iran "economically bigger, better, and stronger than ever before."
On Saturday, in an address to the nation, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Trump's demand is a "dream they should send to their grave."
A week ago, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and killed various government officials, including the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, in strikes.
In retaliation for the attacks, Iran has bombed Middle Eastern countries including Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, according to SBS News.
In the Saturday address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for attacks on regional countries, Jakarta Globe reported.
The Globe also reported that 1,230 people were killed in Iran and that six US troops were killed.
Leavitt has stated that the war would likely last four to six weeks.

items.title: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

s: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday.
As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas.
This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.
The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards.
With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia.
One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged.
As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas.

He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.
In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively.
These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member.
Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.

items.title: Caloundra win round 3 game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra have won their round 3 Football Queensland Premier League 2 game against Pine Hills 5 goals to 2 at Meridan Plains, Queensland, Australia on Sunday.
"Two [wins] from three [games]" said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"I think we'll probably be in the top four now.
Not a bad start.
It's still very early days.
Yeah, you can't get too ahead of yourselves.
I think you've just got to take it week by week for the moment."
Riley Campbell opened the scoring for Caloundra in the second minute.
Aaron Doherty levelled the score two minutes later.
Alex Witte took Pine Hills ahead in the eleventh minute.
Darryl Barton brought the scores level again in the thirteenth minute.
Barton scored his second goal to retake the lead do Caloundra in the twenty seventh minute.
Caloundra lead three goals to two at the break.
Jake Debbage added Caloundra's fourth in the fifty first minute before Mackenar Bradfield took the score line to five goals to three in the ninetieth minute.
"It was a pretty even game, first half," said Pine Hills assistant coach Daniel Cunha.
"[We] conceded three goals.
Lazy goals, in our opinion.
But we managed to bounce back with two goals.
Managed to stay in the game, but yeah, second half with early, conceded early goals, so that was it for us."
Caloundra host Mitchellton on Saturday, while Pine Hills travel to Samford.

items.title: "One Battle After Another" wins 6 Oscars including Best Picture

s: One Battle After Another was the big winner at the 98th Academy Awards ceremony, held on Sunday, March 15 at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, California.
The film received six Oscars including Best Picture.
Director Paul Thomas Anderson personally won Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay, in addition to being one of the producers who received the Best Picture award.

The other three Oscars which One Battle After Another received were for Best Editing and Best Casting, the first time the latter award has been presented, and for Sean Penn as Best Supporting Actor, the third Oscar of his career.
Sinners, which had set a record by earning sixteen Oscar nominations, won awards in four categories: Best Actor for Michael B.
Jordan, Best Original Screenplay for Ryan Coogler, Best Original Score for Ludwig Goransson, and Best Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw.
Arkapaw is the first woman to win an Academy Award for Best Cinematography.
Two other films won multiple Oscars.
Frankenstein won Best Production Design, Best Costume Design, and Best Makeup and Hairstyling.
KPop Demon Hunters won Best Animated Feature and Best Song for Golden.
Best Supporting Actress: Amy Madigan for Weapons
Best International Feature: Sentimental Value, from Norway (directed by Joachim Trier)
Best Visual Effects: Avatar: Fire and Ash
Best Documentary Feature: Mr. Nobody Against Putin
Best Documentary Short: All the Empty Rooms
Best Animated Short: The Girl Who Cried Pearls
Best Live Action Short: The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva (tie)
The Oscar ceremony was hosted by Conan O'Brien.

items.title: South Korean military halts small firearms drills after stray bullet strikes young girl on playground

s: On Tuesday, officials for the South Korean Army said at a press conference that they were suspending all scheduled drills involving smaller firearms such as rifles and handguns.

The decision was made in response to an incident earlier in the week on Monday that resulted in a young girl at a children playground in Daegu being injured near the neck by an alleged stray bullet from a military drill at nearby military facility.
Her injuries were not life-threatening and she was released from the hospital.
Her name was not released to the general public.
Investigations into the circumstances leading up the incident were said to be underway.
The incident raised questions regarding the military's practice of conducting shooting drills in close proximity to civilian territory.
A spokesperson for the army confirmed that a firearms drill had indeed been taking place at the same time the girl reported being struck.
The incident came a year after the South Korean Army accidentally bombed a small village near the North Korean border, injuring 30 civilians, while conducting a drill with US forces.

items.title: Musique Libre Femmes plays for Women's History Month at Tompkins Square Library in New York City

s: On Thursday, March 12, 2026, the Tompkins Square Library in New York City hosted a concert by Musique Libre Femmes, in its basement performance space.
This performance featured Cheryl Pyle on flute, Ayumi Ishito on saxophones, and Roberta Piket on piano.
There were approximately fifteen people in attendance.
Wikinews attended the event and took several photos and recordings to transcribe for this news report.
The performance started at 6:00 p.m.
New York Time (2200 UTC), and was introduced by director of adult services Jeffrey Katz.
After explaining that the series was ongoing, and announcing upcoming performance dates as well, he introduced the performers:
((Jeffrey Katz)) So we are celebrating Women's History Month with Musique Libre Femmes.
And this is a group of all women free jazz improvisers who compose, create spontaneous, in-the-moment music.
The group consists of some of the most experienced improvisers of the New York Jazz scene.
And they have recently played at the Lady Got Chops Festival, the Downtown Music Gallery, and many of the New York City Jazz venues.
After which, the performance began and lasted about forty minutes, after which the audience applauded.
After the event, Pyle had the following comments about the series:

((Cheryl Pyle)) I started the group Musique Libre Femmes, Free Music Women, because I saw a film called Fire Music, and they interviewed Carla Bley and Ingrid Sertso, and they didn't talk about any of their music.
And they didn't talk about any other women improvisers, Barbara Donald, you know, anybody.
So I wanted to do some concerts with all women.
((CP)) And today we played with Roberta Piket on piano and Ayumi Ishito on tenor sax and soprano sax and myself, Cheryl Pyle on C-flute, piccolo and alto flute.
And we're here at the Tompkins Square Library in the East Village and we just had a wonderful concert.

items.title: United States announces blockade on the Strait of Hormuz

s: On Sunday, United States President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that the US is imposing a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Trump, the blockade was in effect as of 10:00 a.m.
Eastern Time (1400 UTC).
The blockade was imposed following the collapse of talks held in Islamabad between the United States and Iran.
"Effective immediately, the United States Navy, the finest in the world, will be BLOCKADING any and all ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz," Trump declared.
According to The Guardian, oil prices briefly rose above US$100 a barrel following news of the blockade, before easing back to just over US$99; gas prices also increased.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf posted on X to "Enjoy the current pump figures.
With the so-called 'blockade', soon you'll be nostalgic for $4–$5 gas.
He further stated that Iran would respond in kind to both escalation and diplomacy, warning that it would "fight" if confronted militarily but would "deal with logic" if approached constructively.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed hope that the ceasefire would remain stable, stating that Beijing is willing to cooperate with all parties to "guarantee the uninterrupted flow of energy supplies," and that stability in the Strait of Hormuz is critically important to China.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV visits four nations in Africa

s: Pope Leo XIV arrived by plane in Algeria on Monday, April 13, beginning his apostolic visit to Africa.

A senior Vatican official told the BBC the pope wanted to "turn the world's attention to Africa"; the BBC reported the eleven-day visit would address themes of peace, migration, and interfaith dialogue.
The trip also includes stops in Cameroon, Angola, and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit marked Leo's second major foreign trip as pope since his election in May last year.
The regions of the continent being visited are among the quickest growing in Catholicism in the world.
There were an estimated 288 million Catholics in Africa in 2024, making up more than one-fifth of the world's total.
His first stop in Algeria marked the first papal visit to the country in history.
While there, Leo planned to visit several locations including ancient Christian sites in Annaba and the Great Mosque of Algiers in the capital before departing.

The stop was followed by a visit to Cameroon, where Leo addressed about 120,000 people in Douala, encouraging young people to turn away from violence and corruption and advocating for justice and peace.
He was expected to make a planned visit to a Catholic hospital in the city before traveling to Yaoundé to meet with students from the Catholic University of Central Africa.
On Sunday, April 19, the pope arrived in Angola, where he met with President João Lourenço and other officials.
He later addressed a crowd gathered near the capital, Luanda.
He was also expected to visit the town of Muxima, the country's main Christian pilgrimage site.

After Angola, the pope arrived on Tuesday, April 21, in Equatorial Guinea, where, according to the BBC, Catholics make up more than 70% of the central African nation, for the final leg of the visit, before his scheduled return to the Vatican.

items.title: Wikimedia Foundation closes Wikinews after 21 years

s: The Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation announced on March 30 its decision to close all language editions of the project.

In the announcement, a representative from Wikimedia Foundation cited motivations such as "long-term sustainability, levels of community activity, and the availability of reliable news coverage on other platforms".
The announcement stated that all Wikinews editions—referring to the multiple language sections of Wikinews—would "transition to read-only mode" on May 4.
The announcement did not mention the time zone when the wiki would go in read-only mode; but Wikinews operated under the UTC timezone.

In the announcement message, WMF trustee Victoria Doronina said, "We thank all contributors who have participated in Wikinews over the years and helped build a unique experiment in collaborative journalism within the Wikimedia movement.
We understand that some of them may be disappointed by this decision.
To our regret, the project wasn't able to fulfil its promise, and many of its functions were eclipsed by the notable news coverage in Wikipedias."
According to the WMF, most traffic to Wikinews came in the form of web crawlers and bots, as opposed to humans.
Per the Wikimedia Cloud statistics in the past one year, both, English and Chinese Wikinews received more traffic from humans as compared to crawlers.
The foundation stated in its closure recommendation that it is "difficult to claim that it is disseminating educational content and, even more so, that it is doing so effectively and globally."
On March 31, users from different countries and regions started discussions regarding moving the Wikinews content and community to another website at Wikimedia's Meta-Wiki.

Miraheze and Wikimedia NYC were in discussion of continuing the hosting as Wikinews Pulse, with a restructure to increase multilingual support and try new outputs, according to a note by a Wikimedia volunteer User:Pharos.
However, at the time of publishing this report, they had not provided an estimated time the project would be restarted.
Wikinews was a sister project of other Wikimedia initiatives.
Some of the other sister projects includes Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wikimedia Commons.
All of these Wikimedia projects support the dissemination of free knowledge and media.
The future of Wikinews was raised for consideration in June, with a WMF task force recommending the project's closure, followed by a period of public consultation about Wikinews.
After this process, the Board announced in March that the 31 active editions of Wikinews would be placed in read-only mode indefinitely.
Wikinews was launched in November 2004.
It was first proposed by an anonymous contributor in January 2003 and faced a community vote that ended 151 yea and 59 nay, leading to the first demo going live in October 2004.
The English-language Wikinews was formally created December 2 of that year, with German following one day later.
The project's early development followed a series of community discussions and milestones in late 2004 and early 2005.
A non-binding straw poll on content licensing began on October 26, 2004, alongside discussions on the project's scope and policies.
The initial demo site, hosted at demo.wikinews.org, was later moved to the English Wikinews domain on December 2 of that year.

Following the launch of the English and German editions in December 2004, additional language editions were created in early 2005, including Dutch, French, Swedish, Spanish, Bulgarian, Polish, Romanian, and Portuguese.
The project also adopted a logo in February 2005 through a community voting process.
While many Wikinews articles were synthesized from other news sources, the project also posted original reporting.
The purpose of this activity was to add exclusive content which would not be available elsewhere on the web or on television.
These original reports included interviews with people such as Shimon Peres, then-president of Israel; U.S.
Senator Sam Brownback; journalist Gay Talese; and voice actor Billy West.
A 2005 article featuring original reporting, Unrest in Belize, was cited by Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales as Wikinews's first scoop.

items.title: Opposition leader Tarique Rahman returns to Bangladesh after 17 years

s: Tarique Rahman, the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, landing in Dhaka after 17 years in self-imposed exile in London.
His arrival marks a significant development in the country's political landscape following the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.
Rahman is the son of Khaleda Zia, the official chairperson of the party and former Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
Upon landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Rahman was greeted by thousands of Bangladesh Nationalist Party supporters amid tight security.

Accompanied by his wife, Zubaida Rahman, and daughter, Zaima Rahman, he addressed a rally, emphasizing national unity, inclusivity across religious lines, and the vision of a democratic and economically strong Bangladesh.
He drew parallels to the country's 1971 war of independence.
Rahman, aged 60, left Bangladesh in 2008 for medical treatment after being released on bail following 18 months in detention during the military-backed government's rule from 2006 to 2008.
He was convicted in absentia of charges including corruption, money laundering, and involvement in a 2004 grenade attack on a political rally for his political rival, Sheikh Hasina.
These convictions were overturned or stayed after Hasina's government's fall.
His return comes amid preparations for general elections scheduled for early 2026, under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.
The elections follow a student-led uprising in 2024 that resulted in Hasina's removal and her subsequent flight to India.
The protests, initially sparked by opposition to a job quota system, escalated into broader anti-government demonstrations, leading to an estimated 1,400 deaths according to United Nations figures.
Hasina has since been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the crackdown.
According to a December poll by the International Republican Institute, the BNP is the frontrunner for the election with 30 percent support.
The party has recently distanced itself from allies like Jamaat-e-Islami to adopt a more centrist approach.
However, challenges remain, including integrating party factions, maintaining law and order, and addressing potential unrest from Awami League supporters.
The Awami League was not allowed to participate in the elections.
Rahman's mother, Khaleda Zia, 80, is hospitalised in critical condition since November 2025.
She was the BNP's acting chairman since 2018 and was jailed most of the times during Hasina's administration.

items.title: United States capture Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro

s: The president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, has been captured by the United States on Saturday at around 3 am UTC-4, according to a post by US president Donald Trump on social media.
Trump has told reporters Maduro had been “in a house that was more like a fortress”, in the country’s capital, Caracas.
Trump justified this action by claiming that Maduro is the leader of the Cartel de los Soles, and pushing illegal immigration of dangerous individuals in the United States.
Yván Gil Pinto, Venezuela’s foreign minister, said the country has requested a United Nations Security Council meeting to be held after the attack.
The BBC reports airstrikes in Caracas targeting La Carlota, an airbase and Fort Tiuna, a military base where the United States suspected Maduro to be located, and in other locations.
According to local authorities there has been civilian deaths and injuries, but the exact numbers are still unknown.
It was also reported by the BBC that the operation was orchestrated by a {CIA infiltration of the Venezuelan government.
France 24 reported that the CIA had been monitoring his “every movement since August”, despite Maduro’s efforts to change location regularly.
It was also reported that the operation involved more than 150 military aircraft, including one helicopter that was to capture Maduro.

According to the United States authorities, the Delta Force special operation force, arrived at Maduro’s location at “2:01 a.m. local time” and were able to capture him before he could get into his solid steel safe room (sources contradict however, on his exact location at that point.
Some sources reported that Trump said Maduro was almost in his safe room whilst others said he was sleeping in his bed).
They then relocated the “indicted persons” on a ship after crossing the coastline of Venezuela at 3:29 am.

Trump later revealed that Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, was also captured, and both were on board the USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) with destination the southern district of New York, ultimately to be prosecuted.

Attorney General Pam Bondi was quoted by the BBC saying “[he will] face the full wrath of American justice on American soil in American courts” and, according to CNN, announced an indictment for leading “state‐sponsored gangs” and supporting drug trafficking.
Venezuelan authorities also reported other strikes, said to be made with the intent of seizing their oil and minerals, and have declared national emergency.
They, along with Cuba, Colombia, Iran and Russia, have denounced the action as a “serious military aggression”.
Argentine’s president, Javier Milei supported the action.
Venezuela’s vice‐president, Delcy Rodríguez called for Maduro and his wife to be released, saying the operation violated the country’s territorial integrity.
The BBC stated that these strikes follow a string of more than 30 strikes on Venezuelan vessels, and a strike on a “dock area” in Maracaibo, resulting in the death of more than 110 people.
The Trump administration stated that it is engaging in “non‐international armed conflict with […] alleged drug traffickers”.
According to the BBC, legal experts doubt the legality of these actions, saying the strikes are not against "lawful military targets".
According to CNN, Trump also justified not advising Congress before the operation to avoid a "leak", which drew criticisms from Democratic lawmakers.

After the capture, the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against Maduro in which Maduro and others were charged with “conspiracy to commit narco‐terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine”.

According to the BBC, Maduro has denied this and has said before that Trump’s actual goal is to get access to Venezuela’s oil reserves, as indicated by the United States’ confiscation of several oil tankers.

items.title: Kyiv street to be named for former Ukrainian parliament chairman Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv

s: A street in Kyiv will be named after the former Speaker of the Parliament Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv.
The initiative to commemorate the prominent Ukrainian politician was supported by 57% of participants in a public poll on "Kyiv Digital" application.
On January 1, Maryna Poroshenko, the leader of “European Solidarity”, announced the street name in the Kyiv City Council and on Facebook.
As the result, a section along Mariinsky Park – from Hrushevskoho Street to Parkova Road – will bear the politician's name, named "Andrei Parubia Street".
In December, former President of Ukraine and head of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko asked the residents of Kyiv to support the vote to name the street after Parubiy.
The street had no name at the time of the proposal.
"This place is significant for our team and for Andriy himself — a significant part of his journey is connected with it," Poroshenko said.
On October 1, 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree awarding Parubiy the title of Hero of Ukraine.

A petition to award the title of Hero of Ukraine to Parubiy was registered on the presidential website on September 2, gaining 25,000 signatures, which was necessary for the proposal to be considered by President.
The Verkhovna Rada, the Ukrainian parliament, also supported the request.
Parubiy was among several people who were conferred Heroes of Ukraine.
Others were writer Volodymyr Vakulenko and student and footballer Stepan Chubenko.
Poroshenko lauded the decision, recalling that "Parubiy dedicated his entire life to serving Ukraine".
Andriy Parubiy, 54, who served as the Chairman of Verkhovna Rada from 14 April 2016 to 29 August 2019, was shot and killed in Lviv on 30 August 2025.
He died at the scene from injuries.
The killing happened amid the Russian invasion, which started in 2022.
The shooter managed to escape.
Later, Ukrainian authorities detained a suspect, and allege there is a Russian link to the killing.
Parubiy was an active participant of Euromaidan.
He also served as Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine from February till August 2014.
The suspected killer of Ukrainian lawmaker Andriy Parubiy admitted on 2 September his role in the killing.
He claimed to have comitted the crime in an act of "revenge" against the country’s authorities.
He denied having worked with Russian special services.

items.title: "I came to be the manager ... not the coach": Manchester United fire head coach Ruben Amorim

s: On Monday, Manchester United football team fired its coach Ruben Amorim after fourteen months in the role.
Amorim had met with Omar Berrada, chief executive officer of the team, and Jason Wilcox, the team's director of football, on Friday morning.
While discussing his preferred 3-4-3 style, the conversation reportedly quickly spiraled out of control, resulting in Amorim losing his job.
Manchester United announced the news of the dismissal at around 10 a.m. on Monday.
After the team drawing against Leeds F.C.
1-1, the coach had said at a press conference that he came to be "the manager, not the coach" and said Wilcox should "do his job".
Wilcox intended the meeting to focus on the recent draw.

Manchester United was sixth in the Premier League, almost not classifying for the Champions League, less than four points ahead of Sunderland A.F.C., Everton F.C., Fulham F.C., Brighton & Hove Albion F.C., Newcastle United and Brentford F.C., a precarious position, El Pais reported.
Former Manchester United captain Gary Neville communicated to Sky Sports News that he expected better performance, saying he "thought they'd get through another couple of weeks."

items.title: Homeland Security says Minneapolis woman shot by ICE officer dies

s: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported Wednesday that a woman shot by a U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis has died.
Homeland Security officials have described the shooting as an act of self-defense, while Minnesota governor Tim Walz and Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey have pushed back on this account.

DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin stated that the shooting occurred when ICE officers fired "defensive shots" in response to the woman "attempting to run over our law enforcement officers" with her vehicle.
Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said the woman’s conduct was "an act of domestic terrorism."
The incident was under active investigation, with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and the FBI taking over the case.
Walz said the state was working to learn more and asked residents to remain calm, while protest activity continued at the scene and a substantial law-enforcement presence remained in the area.
According to ABC News, Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, said in a statement that he was aware of the shooting and urged the agency to depart the city at once.
On social media, he stated the involvement of federal immigration officers was "causing chaos in our city.
He added that the city is "demanding ICE to leave the city immediately," and said officials "stand rock solid with our immigrant and refugee communities.
In a news conference, he disputed the account that the woman's vehicle was weaponized against the agent.

items.title: Roblox player uncovers cheating, awarded Guinness World Record

s: In early January, international media reported that Quinten Delaere, an 18-year-old, had been officially recognized by Guinness World Records after exposing cheating on the Roblox platform.
